summary: A 1973 memo reporting what a small informal meeting at UCLA concluded about the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol. It covers transfers between two remote servers, site-dependent information, and nitpicks about earlier FTP proposals (RFC 354, 385 and 414). It is a discussion paper, not a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 430 reports discussion at an informal FTP meeting in January 1973. Participants considered how two servers could transfer a file, how FTP should describe file types, and how users could provide host-specific storage information.

questions: what is the ftp getsocket command
subtitle: A report on a 1973 FTP meeting about server transfers, file types, and site-specific parameters.

tldr.problem: Participants saw unclear points in FTP, a lack of a defined way for two FTP servers to transfer files directly, and difficulty expressing host-specific file-system settings.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reports meeting comments, proposes multi-character TYPE codes, supports the general server-server model in RFC 438, and discusses where to place site-specific storage parameters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 430 records discussion and proposals from an informal meeting. It does not specify a final FTP extension.

facts.value: A, AP, E, EP, I, L

sections.title: The FTP Meeting and Its Questions
sections.content:
On January 23, 1973, four participants met informally at UCLA to discuss FTP. RFC 430 reports their consensus and disagreements about server-server transfers, site-dependent information, and earlier FTP documents RFCs 354, 385, and 414. The meeting also discussed print files, which RFC 430 says are treated separately in RFC 448.

The memo includes comments on command-response wording, block-mode header and restart-marker definitions, EBCDIC text mode, password changes, and whether sending TYPE before BYTE should be a recommendation or a server restriction.
sections.plainLanguage: The meeting reviewed unclear or disputed parts of FTP and considered ways to make them easier to use. The memo records discussion rather than issuing a final specification.

sections.title: FTP Type Codes and Character Sets
sections.content:
The memo notes that print-file status is independent of character encoding, such as ASCII or EBCDIC. It therefore describes at least four combinations of character code and print-file status. The authors propose using multiple letters in the TYPE command instead of a separate single character for every combination.

The proposed letters are A for ASCII, E for EBCDIC, P for print file, I for image, and L for local byte. The legal example types are A, AP, E, EP, I, and L. The memo says text mode is not possible for EBCDIC-coded files, while stream and block modes work.
sections.plainLanguage: A file can be both EBCDIC and a print file, so the memo proposes combining type letters. For example, EP means EBCDIC and print file.

sections.title: Transfers Between Two FTP Servers
sections.content:
RFC 438 proposes a controller process that connects to FTP servers at two sites, asks each server to reserve a data socket, and passes the socket names between them. The servers then establish a data connection and transfer the file without routing the file data through the controller's host.

RFC 430 endorses that general model and proposes a more symmetrical approach. It suggests that a user FTP should not have to listen before a transfer command, and proposes a GETSocket command that returns a send/receive pair. The controller would pass socket numbers to the opposite servers with SOCK commands, after which transfer commands start the exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller asks each server for socket numbers and tells the servers about each other. The two servers can then establish the data connection and exchange the file.

sections.title: Host-Specific File Parameters
sections.content:
Some host file systems need settings that FTP commands do not express. The memo gives IBM systems as an example. CCN tried using default mappings for each FTP type, mode, and structure combination, but found too few combinations and difficult-to-remember rules. Some mappings could also change data in a way that could not be reversed, such as truncating records to 80 bytes.

CCN planned friendly defaults that stored most input invertibly, plus keywords on STOR such as SOURCE or FORT and fuller DD parameters for advanced users. The memo discusses putting these in a generalized pathname, using an ALLO command, or using a server-dependent command such as SRVR.
sections.plainLanguage: A server may need local storage details that FTP does not carry. The memo discusses adding optional keywords or parameters so users can supply those details.
